parole.testo: Borrowed from Old East Slavic адамантъ (adamantŭ), ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas). See the more modern form deimantas, from the same source through French.
Borrowed from Old East Slavic отвернь (otvernĭ).
Derived from the adverb advernai (“backwards”), itself from Old East Slavic отвернь (otvernĭ).

parole.significato: church (building used for worship by Christians); (greater than usually) basilica
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old East Slavic божница (božnica, “church, capel”), probably specifically from the dialectal form бозьница (bozĭnica) (cf. Proto-Slavic *božьnica, Belarusian бажніца (bažnica, “shelf with icons; house of prayer”), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *bogъ (“god”) or *božьnъ (“divine”). Cognat
Borrowed from Old East Slavic колода (koloda), from Proto-Slavic *kolda.
Borrowed from Old East Slavic [Term?], itself probably borrowed from Proto-Finnic *kirstu.
Borrowed from Old East Slavic капуста (kapusta). Compare Polish kapusta, Russian капу́ста (kapústa).
Borrowed from Old East Slavic лѧхъ (lęxŭ), from the name of the Lendians tribe, from Proto-Slavic *lęděninъ. Compare Hungarian lengyel.
Ultimately from Old East Slavic недѣлꙗ (nedělja), possibly via Belarusian нядзе́ля (njadzjélja). Compare Estonian nädal, Latgalian nedeļa, Latvian nedēļa, Livonian nädīļ, Samogitian nedielė.
Borrowed from Old East Slavic смыкъ (smykŭ).
Borrowed from Old East Slavic търгъ (tŭrgŭ, “trade, trading, commerce; (trade) square”), from Proto-Slavic *tъrgъ. Compare Latvian tìrgus.

From name of Vladimir the Great (958—1015) (who subdued Yotvingians in 983). * Per Būga (1912), from *Valadýmieras + valdõvas (“ruler”), valdýti (“to rule”), from Old East Slavic Володимѣръ (Volodiměrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *Voldiměrъ. Possibly via Yotvingian. Compare Proto-Germanic *kaisaraz < Latin
